title: Forcing Positional Weaknesses | Sicilian Defense | GM Naroditsky’s Top Theory Speedrun
openingName: Sicilian Defense (vs the Bc4 Italian setup)

moves.spoken: White plays the bishop to c4 — popular below master level because players default to their anti-e5 Italian moves. Against this Sicilian setup it's ineffective, and the reason is one word: e6.
e6 completely blunts the c4 bishop and makes it look silly — and a later d5 can come with tempo.
To punish the bishop fully we strike with d5, seizing the center with tempo.
The light-squared bishop's placement dictates our whole development. We can't lead with the dark bishop — it would drop d5 — so we bring the g8-knight out first.
teaches: let the key piece decide the move order

moves.spoken: The knight to f6 is natural — the knight to e7 would just block in the dark-squared bishop. Don't rediscover the wheel; put the pieces on normal squares.
c4 is White's first real error — a weakening move that pretends to fight for the center but only helps us.
We take on c4, and though it opens White's bishop, it leaves him with a backward pawn on d2 and an open d-file to lean on — and we get the open-center game the Sicilian wants.
teaches: open the center; saddle White with a backward d-pawn

moves.spoken: The bishop goes to its most active square, d6 — and it's safe, because if White tries to fix the weakness with d4, everything trades and the bishop check on b4 picks up his queen.
teaches: Bd6 works: the Bb4+ trade-down motif

moves.spoken: White plays d3, and now we combine development with prophylaxis.
h6 stops White's bishop from reaching g5 — quiet, Petrosian-style prophylaxis. And there's no fear of a sac on h6 with White so undeveloped.

The bishop to g4 pins, and it's especially juicy because the pawn on d3 denies White the Be2 unpin — the pin simply sticks. Now we threaten the knight into d4 or e5, either of which lets us capture on f3 and wreck White's kingside pawns.
teaches: a pin White can’t break, then Nd4/Ne5 to smash f3
